newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sugar trade concerned by fraud-busting plans.
newsitem.headline: EU sugar trade concerned by fraud-busting plans.

text.p: European sugar traders said on Friday they were very worried about fraud, especially in eastern Europe, but counter-measures planned by the European Commission could prove ruinous.
"Our major concern is fraud," Hannelore Mill, Secretary General of the European Sugar Trade Association (ASSUC), told Reuters in an interview.
But measures planned by the Commission seemed to be totally disproportionate to the amount of fraud and could ruin sugar exporters, she added.
In 1996, there were 31 reported cases of sugar fraud amounting to 1.2 million Ecus - mostly in Germany, Spain and Britain - according to a Commission annual report.
That compared with 1,944 cases of reported agricultural fraud in 1996 totalling 203.8 million Ecus, mainly in cereals, olive oil, milk and beef.
On Monday, the EU's trade mechanisms committee is due to discuss draft plans requiring exporters to provide proof of arrival of sugar shipments and consumption in the country of destination.
"It's an enormous burden on exporters and could ruin companies," Mill said.
Mill said opinions were sharply divided.
One group, including major sugar exporting countries, favours maintaining the current system under which exporters are no longer responsible for sugar shipments once the vessels leave EU territory.

Another group, including various factions in the Commission, wants to make traders responsible for any sugar finding its way back into the EU and to make them repay export refunds. Traders would be responsible for providing proof of arrival and use.

Mill said sugar should be treated differently because, unlike other products covered by the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), it was self-financed by sugar processors and beet growers through a production levy and was no burden on the EU budget.
Sugar fraud surged in 1989 after the collapse of the Berlin wall and eastern Europe started to pursue free market policies.
"They didn't know the (EU's) rules," Mill said, adding that the Commission would have to undertake a major information campaign before eastern European countries join the EU.

For instance EU subsidised sugar was exported to the Czech republic and then sold into Slovakia for use in biscuits, preserves and other processed products which would then be re-exported to the EU at zero duty under preferential agreements.
The European Commission would then demand that EU sugar traders pay back the export subsidies.
Another example was transit trade through the EU involving eastern European countries, such as Poland and the Czech Republic, and Morocco and other North African countries.

Around 50,000 tonnes a year of Polish and Czech sugar never reached its destination but remained in Spain, lured by higher EU guaranteed prices aimed at attracting supplies to cover the country's sugar deficit.
